item.title: The Fare to Nowhere
item.description: Every night the app freezes for four seconds, and every night a silent passenger sits a little closer to the driver's seat. Douglas Whitlow has a cold flask, a dead address, and a growing suspicion that his rider has never wanted to arrive.
item.content:encoded:
The request came in at twenty past eleven, on a wet Tuesday night in October, and I accepted it because I had been parked outside the Harcastle Co-operative for forty minutes with nothing but a cold flask for company. The pickup pin sat at the far end of Harcastle Road, where the street lamps give out and the road drops towards the railway cutting. I had never been given a fare there. The estimate was eleven minutes away.

I drove it in nine. The rain came in sideways off the allotments, and the wipers on my Skoda have never cleared more than the middle two-thirds of the glass. At the underpass I slowed, as I always do, because the road narrows there and the brick sweats. The work phone sat clamped in its mount on the dashboard, and the pin on its screen showed a blue dot, then a blue dot with a ring around it, then the word *Arriving*.

Then the screen froze.

I have driven for the app for three years and I know its habits. It stalls in the cutting and under the rail bridge; it stalls whenever a lorry parks too close to the mast on Fenner Lane. A frozen screen is nothing. The map goes grey, the little car stops turning, and the radio carries on without it. I put the handbrake on and counted, as one does. One. Two. The heater ticked. Three. Somewhere behind me a drainpipe was emptying itself onto the tarmac.

Four, and the display came back, and the rear door was shut.

I had not heard it open. I want to be exact about this. I heard no latch, no change in the weight of the car on its springs, no rush of rain. But the interior light was off, as I had left it, and in the mirror there was a man sitting directly behind me, hands folded on his knees, a hat on his lap.

"Good evening," he said. "I'm sorry to have kept you."

"Mr Drummond?" I said, because the app said so. *Harold D., 4.9 stars.* There was no photograph.

"That's right."

He was perhaps sixty. His face had the colour of wet slate, not ill, exactly, but finished with colour, and his raincoat was dry. I noticed that at once and decided not to notice it. The coat was of a cut my father wore. The hat on his knee was a flat cap, and it was dry as well.

"Where are we heading?"

He gave me an address: *Number nine, Wick Yard, off the Harcastle Road.* I typed it. The app considered it and returned a small red line of text. *Address not found.* I tried it without the number, then without the yard. Nothing. I said so, apologetically, and offered to use my own map.

"You won't need it," said Mr Drummond. "Keep to the road. I shall tell you." He settled back. "You mustn't mind the quiet, Mr Whitlow. I'm not much for conversation."

I had not told him my name. It was on the dashboard card, of course, in the little plastic window, and I told myself that.

I released the handbrake. The display was still lit, and in the corner, where the bars of signal should have been, there was a single grey dash. Beside it, in type too small to read, the app had begun to count something upwards.

In the mirror, Mr Drummond was sitting very still. It seemed to me that the back seat was a little narrower than it had been.

• • •

I drove on because there was nothing else to do. Mr Drummond named the turnings a half-second before I reached them, *left here, now the second right*, in a voice with no weight behind it, and at the end of Wick Yard there was no Number nine. There was a wall, a drain, and a sodium lamp that had been dead long enough to grow moss. I stopped. When I turned in my seat the back was empty, the leather dry, the cushion not even dented. The work phone gave three bars of signal and a rating request. I did not give one.

On Wednesday the account asked for me again.

*Harold D.* The pickup was the Harcastle Road underpass, where the concrete takes every bar from the screen, and I told myself I would cancel. My thumb was on the button when everything stopped. The picture did not go black. It held, bright and perfectly still, and the clock in the corner stopped at 22:41. I heard the rear door close. Nothing had opened it.

"Good evening, Mr Whitlow."

He sat behind the passenger headrest now, no longer in the middle. I could see the flat cap in the corner of the mirror, and one grey ear. "Mr Drummond," I said. "What is it you want? Where is it you want to go?" He said, "Keep to the road." The clock moved. 22:42. I drove him through four miles of wet streets that led, as before, to nothing. He spoke only to direct me. When I asked a third time what he wanted, he looked out of the window as a man does who has been asked something rude.

On Thursday I took the pickup in the car park behind the Harcastle Infirmary, which has been shuttered since the spring, with plywood across the casualty doors and a single fox watching me from the ambulance bay. I had decided to keep both hands on the wheel and not turn. The display froze again. I counted. At four seconds the cold arrived at my right shoulder, the way a draught arrives from a door you thought was shut, and a hand came down upon the console between the seats.

It was a large hand, grey as the face, the nails cut square. It lay beside the gear stick with the fingers a little spread, patient, exactly where a driver rests his own. There was a gold ring on it, worn thin. A faint smell came with it, and I knew it before I could name it: engine oil, and pipe tobacco, and the inside of an old coat.

"Mr Drummond," I said, and my voice did something I had not permitted it to do. "Please. What do you want?"

He did not answer. He was looking, I think, at the wheel. I could feel him looking at the place where my hands were.

The picture thawed. 23:17. A single bar of signal came back, and the app, with its usual cheerfulness, congratulated me on a ride completed.

The hand was still on the console. It stayed there for the whole drive home, and I did not once look down. When I parked outside Alder Close and switched off the engine, I sat a long minute listening to the rain, and then I heard the rear door open and close, quietly, and I understood that he had stepped out first.

• • •

I did not telephone anyone that night. I sat in the kitchen with the lights on and the back door locked and a cup of tea I never drank. At some point after two the cup was cold, and I found I had been watching the chair opposite me.

In the morning I rang the driver support line from the bottom of the garden, standing among the wet bean poles. It seemed to me that a thing which could follow a car might not follow a signal as far as a shed. I used the house phone, the cordless one, carried down the path with its aerial out. The work phone, the one that ran the app, I had left in my coat pocket on the hook by the shed door.

There was a menu. There was a recording that told me my call was important. After eleven minutes a young woman took my driver number and my name, asked me to describe the issue, and listened to the description with the courteous blankness of someone reading from a card. She said she would put me through to a supervisor. The line clicked twice.

"Hargreaves," said a man. "Vernon Hargreaves. Go ahead, Mr Whitlow."

His voice was flat and unhurried, a voice with the edges planed off. I told him everything: the Tuesday request, the four seconds, the man in the back, the three nights since, the hand on the console. I said the account name twice, and spelled it. I heard him typing, slow, two fingers by the sound of it.

"There's no Drummond," he said. "Not as a rider, not as a driver. No account under that name, no trips to or from Alder Close with that profile. I've pulled your history for the last fourteen days. Every fare you've taken is matched to a named passenger with a payment on file."

"Then look at Harcastle Road," I said. "The underpass. The car park behind the infirmary."

More typing. Somewhere behind him a door closed, and the sound of it went on a little too long, as if the room were larger than a room ought to be.

"What I have," said Vernon, "is you. You've been logged in for six hours, Mr Whitlow. Same stretch of Harcastle Road. Your location hasn't moved since eleven last night, and your status has not changed. It still shows you available." He paused. "Are you at the car now?"

"I'm in my garden."

"Yes," he said. "That's what's odd about it."

I waited for him to suggest a doctor, or a rest. He did neither. The typing had stopped, and the line carried only the thin sound of an open connection, the sound of a long corridor. I counted nine seconds. I was going to say his name when he spoke again, and his voice had lost its flatness. It had become careful.

"I'm going to tell you something that is not in the script. I looked at the wrong screen. The account exists. It was never deleted, only flagged, and I am looking at the flag now." A breath. "Harold Drummond. He drove a cab on Harcastle Road for twenty-two years, and in November 1987 he went out on a wet night and was not seen again. The cab was never found. The account was opened for him afterwards, Mr Whitlow. Opened. Nobody here can tell me by whom."

"That is not possible," I said, and heard how little it was worth.

"There's a note on the flag. Head office has been told that the application fails in one circumstance only. When a ride is marked completed that was never started." The corridor sound swelled behind him. "Mr Whitlow, did your app congratulate you last night?"

I did not answer. Down by the fence the bean poles ticked in the wind, and in the coat on the hook the work phone, which I had not touched, gave a single soft chime.

• • •

I did not answer the supervisor. I let the line run on, the corridor sound and Vernon Hargreaves breathing in it. I took the work phone out of the coat on the hook and read what it said. *Trip completed. Thank you for driving, Douglas. You earned £0.00.* There was a rating beneath it, five stars, and no name against it.

"Mr Whitlow?"

"I'm here."

"Then I'll say the rest of it. The logs show your app has dropped out eleven times in three nights. Each time, directly afterwards, the trip is marked complete. Nobody has ever started one." He cleared his throat. "I would not take another request."

I thanked him. I ended the call. I stood among the bean poles with the rain beginning again, and I laid the three nights out in a row, as I would have laid out a week's takings.

He had never wanted to go anywhere. That was the thing I had missed. He had given me an address that was not in the system, and an address that does not exist cannot be reached, and so the journey could never end. That was why he had never once asked me to hurry. He had asked me only to be easy with the silence.

He had moved from the back seat to the headrest, and from the headrest to my shoulder, one reach of the arm at a time. Each reach had been made in the four or five seconds when the display froze and the road stopped being a road. I had taken those seconds for faults. They were the only seconds in which the car belonged to nobody, and he had been using them as a man uses a gap in a hedge.

He was not a passenger. He was a driver who had lost his seat in 1987, on a wet night, on that same stretch of tarmac, and he was working his way back to the wheel.

I ought to have deleted the application. I ought to have sold the car. I did neither, and I have thought since about why, and the honest answer is that I wanted to be certain. A man will walk into a good deal for the sake of certainty.

At ten past eleven that night, with the work phone clipped back into its mount on the dash, it chimed again. *New request. Harcastle Road underpass. 4 min.* The account name was blank.

I drove there with the wipers on their slowest setting. The underpass is two hundred yards of brick and sodium light, with a drain at the lowest point that has been overflowing since the council last mentioned it. I stopped at the mouth, set the handbrake, and looked down into it. The signal bar on the screen had already shrunk to a single stroke. I watched it flicker. The back seat was empty, and the mirror showed me only my own face.

I turned the heater off. I did not want warmth to confuse what came. Then I pressed the button on the side of the handset and held it until it asked whether I was sure, and I said aloud, "Yes," as if someone had asked me.

The screen went black. The little blue light on the mount, which had been lit for three years, went out.

I released the handbrake, put the car into gear and rolled forward into the underpass. Behind me, with no sound of a door, the rear seat took a man's weight and settled.

• • •

The hand on mine was cold in a way I can only call dry. There was no damp in it, though the whole city outside was running with rain. It lay over my knuckles on the gear stick and the weight of it was exact, each finger placed, as a man might rest his hand on a thing he had owned for many years.

I had thought I would speak. I had prepared a sentence in the car park at home, something about what he wanted, and whether he could say it plainly now that there was no signal to interrupt us. I did not say it. The engine idled. The dashboard, which I had not touched, lost its brightness by degrees. First went the clock, then the fuel gauge, then the small orange lamp for the oil. After that the only light came from the sodium lamps at the mouth of the underpass, and then not even that, for the car had rolled further in than I had meant it to.

The seat behind me creaked as it gave up its weight, and the seat beside me creaked as it took it, though I had heard no one pass between. I did not look. I looked at the windscreen, at the brick curving overhead, at the water running down to the drain. I could smell old upholstery and the sweetish stale smell of a cab that has been smoked in for decades. My own car had never smelled of either.

"Mind the quiet," said a voice beside me, mild and dry. "Most don't."

The hand lifted from mine. I heard the click of a seat belt, mine, being undone, and I felt myself rise, or be raised, with no more effort than a coat being taken from a peg. There was a draught of cold air, a door that did not open, and the sound of the gear lever being worked by someone who knew exactly how stiff it was.

Then the screen in its mount, dead a moment before, lit by itself.

The light was white and very bright after the dark. I had to blink before I could read it. I was sitting upright in the back seat, behind the passenger side, where the vinyl was cracked in a long diagonal. Across my chest ran the belt, drawn snug and clicked home by hands that were not mine. I tried my arms. They moved. I did not try the door.

In the driver's seat sat a grey head, bare and narrow, the hair combed flat with something that had dried long ago. Two hands rested on the wheel at ten and two. The wipers began, slowly, on their own. Beyond the glass the underpass was no longer an underpass but a road I did not know, lit and empty, and the rain fell on it without a sound.

The mirror showed me nothing at all. Only the screen spoke, in its small clean letters:

*Trip started. Pickup: 14 Alder Close.*

It was my address. The indicator ticked, left, left, and Harold Drummond drove me home.

item.title: The Larkspur Cylinders
item.description: A bell-ringer takes a garret in a fog-bound lodging house and finds a phonograph cylinder bearing his own voice, begging forgiveness for a drowning he never committed. Each night brings another recording, and every prophecy on them comes true.
item.content:encoded:
The cylinder had been left behind by the man who kept the garret before me. He had gone in the night, owing a fortnight, and had taken his boots and his hat and nothing else. Mr. Wetherby let the room to me on the Tuesday, and on the Wednesday I found the cylinder in the drawer of the washstand, wrapped in a flannel that smelled of camphor and tallow. The label was brown with age. It read, in a thin clerkly hand, *Larkspur, No. 1*.

The phonograph stood on the sill, under the window, its brass horn turned to the room. It had come with the garret, like the damp patch over the bed and the sixth stair that cried out when trodden. I had never wound it. I had my bell to wind, and my father's ledger to puzzle over, and on that night I wanted only to sit and not think of the quarter-day.

The fog had been in the Larkspur since four o'clock. It stood against the glass and gave the lamp a yellow ring, and below me the foghorns on the river called to one another, one low, one lower. I slid the cylinder onto the mandrel. I turned the crank eleven times, because I count what I turn. I lowered the stylus.

First came hissing, and then a breath, taken close.

"Forgive me," said a voice. "Please. I have carried it so long."

It was my voice. I do not say it resembled mine. I know my own voice as I know the weight of the rope in my hands: the flat northern vowels, the catch before a hard consonant. I put my fingers to my throat and felt nothing move there. The speaker went on, tender and low, as a man speaks to a sick child.

"I never meant the water to take him. I held his sleeve as long as I could. You must believe that I held it. Say that you forgive me for the drowning, and I will ask for nothing more."

I stood up. The chair went over behind me. I did not set it right.

There was a silence on the cylinder, and in it the sound of a clock, a slow clock with a loose pendulum, such as hangs in the parlour downstairs. Then a second speaker answered, calm, unhurried, and dry as paper.

"I forgive you, Desmond. Of course I do. Sit down now. It is finished."

It was Mr. Reginald Wetherby. I had heard him on the stairs not two hours before, saying that the gas was not to be wasted. He had said nothing to me of water, or of a sleeve, or of forgiveness. I have never drowned any man. I have never stood on a quay at night and watched a hand go under. I have rung the bell of St. Anselm's every Sunday of my life, and the only thing I have ever dropped into the Mire is a hymn-book.

The stylus ran off the end and clicked, and clicked, and clicked.

I did not lift it. I sat down upon the bed with my hands between my knees and listened to the clicking. The lamp began to gutter. The yellow ring shrank on the glass. And the horn, though it was silent, went on saying *sit down now*.

• • •

I found Mr. Wetherby in the passage by the parlour door the next morning, trimming the wick of the hall lamp with a pair of small silver scissors. I had not slept. I had carried the cylinder down in my coat pocket and I held it out to him in my palm, as one holds out a coin to a beggar one does not trust.

"Someone has been at my machine," I said. "There is a voice on this. It is mine. It speaks of a drowning."

He did not look at the cylinder. He looked at my face, and then he smiled, slowly, with the lips only, and set the scissors down upon the shelf beside the barometer.

"You are pale, Mr. Marchbanks. The fog gets into the sleeping-rooms. I have always said so." He took out his watch and opened it. "The quarter-day is the twenty-fifth. Your father's sum stands at forty-one pounds, six shillings, and I am a patient man, but I am not a charitable one. Good morning."

He went into the parlour. The clock with the loose pendulum began its slow knocking behind the door, and I stood in the passage with the cylinder in my hand until the lamp, which he had trimmed, burned smokeless and steady.

The next night there was another on the sill. It lay in the dust beside the window-catch, brown and fine-ribbed, and the window was latched from within. I told myself I would not play it. I played it before the church clock struck eleven.

It was my voice again, and quieter. It said that the sexton, old Pettigrew, would cough three times during the Tuesday matins, and that the third cough would break the Creed. It said that Mr. Wetherby would stop me on the stairs at noon and name forty-three pounds, not forty-one, for the interest. Then it said, *I did not mean him to go under, Reginald. I took hold of his sleeve. It was wet wool, and it came away in my hand.*

On Tuesday Pettigrew coughed three times, and the third broke the Creed. At noon, on the stairs, a hand touched my elbow, and a dry voice said, "Forty-three pounds, Mr. Marchbanks." I did not answer. I went up and found the fourth cylinder waiting.

So it went for seven days. Each night a brown cylinder; each day its prophecy, kept as faithfully as a tide-table. The cooper's dog; the broken rung of the belfry ladder; the very word Wetherby used for my lateness, which was *negligent*. And between the prophecies the drowning grew. It had a quay now, and a lantern, and the name of the Mire's lock-keeper. It had a boy's cap floating. My own tongue spoke of the hand going under with such tenderness that I caught myself, on the sixth night, with my palm laid flat against the horn as against a cheek.

On the seventh night I did not wind the machine. I sat in the dark and waited, and the stylus lowered itself into the wax of its own accord.

• • •

I carried all seven cylinders to Fothergill's door in the crook of my arm, wrapped in my muffler like a litter of something sickly, and knocked with my knee. It was past one in the morning. He opened at once, in his shirtsleeves, with a pen still in his hand, as though he had been expecting me and had not minded the wait.

"Marchbanks," he said, in the low voice he used for everything, even for the weather. "Come in. You look like a man who has been bailing."

His room was the twin of mine, but warmer. He had a rag rug, a kettle on the hob, and on the table, under a square of green baize, a machine of his own with a japanned horn. I set the cylinders down in a row. I told him what was on them. I told it badly, out of order, the lock-keeper before the cap and the cap before the quay, and he listened with his head a little to one side, nodding, and poured me tea I did not drink.

"Play them," I said. "Play any. Tell me whose voice it is."

He played the first. I watched his face while the wax turned, and there was nothing in it but patience. When the drowning began, the tender plea of Desmond Marchbanks asking pardon, he closed his eyes as a man does at a hymn. Then he lifted the stylus and played the fourth, and the sixth, and let the seventh run until the wet sleeve came away in my hand.

"It is you," he said gently. "I will not pretend otherwise. But think, my dear fellow. Who wound the machine? Who set the cylinder to the horn? Wetherby's is an old man's voice, and an old man's voice is an easy thing to dream."

"Pettigrew coughed three times," I said. "The Creed broke."

"Pettigrew coughs three times every Tuesday. So does the Mire, I sometimes think." He smiled, and laid his hand on the baize. "You walk, Desmond. I have heard your boots on the landing at three in the morning, and your talk through the wall, going on and on. The Larkspur has always made its lodgers strange. The man who had your room before you kept a hat-box of teeth. Sleep, and eat something, and leave the machine alone."

I wanted to believe him. I believed him all the way down the passage, with the muffler empty on my arm, for he had kept the cylinders, saying he would listen to them again by daylight and tell me what he made of it. The key turned stiffly in my door. The lamp, when I lit it, burned low and yellow, and I lay on the bed in my coat with the damp of the Mire coming up through the floorboards.

I did not sleep. Toward four I rose to ease my head against the cold of the window, and the lamp swung my shadow across the room, and I saw the phonograph as I had not seen it in nine days. The brass horn did not point to the room. It lay turned against the wall, its mouth pressed to the paper, canted a hand's breadth out of true, as if it had been set there to listen.

Beneath it, on the boards, lay a small grey drift of plaster dust, fine and fresh and unswept.

I knelt. I put my finger in it. It was still faintly damp.

• • •

I took the horn in both hands and pulled. It came away from the paper with a small dry sound, and a crust of plaster fell across my knuckles. Behind it, where the wall should have been solid, there was a hole the width of a florin, and in the hole the dull gleam of a tin tube, wired to a lath with a twist of copper. I put my ear to it. The tube was cold. It breathed up at me the smell of a coal fire and of tobacco gone stale in a pipe, and from far below, very faint, came the tick of a clock I knew. It was the clock on Wetherby's parlour mantel, the one with the cracked enamel face that he wound each Sunday after chapel.

I stayed there on my knees, and I counted the ticks as I have counted the strokes of the great tenor on a feast day, and somewhere past two hundred I understood.

He had been listening. Not for nine days, but for months. Every night that I had lain in this bed and spoken to my father, or to the water, or to nobody, the tube had carried it down to him, and he had sat in his chair and written it out. I thought of the mornings I had woken with my tongue dry and my throat raw, and had put it down to the damp. I thought of the plea on the cylinder, tender and wheedling: forgive me, Desmond, say you forgive me, say you remember. I knew at last who had spoken it, because I heard it again in my head with the soft vowels laid bare. It was the gentle, patient, reasonable manner of the man who had just sent me to bed with a kind word and my own muffler empty on my arm. Alec Fothergill had begged me to remember. He had begged so sweetly that I had almost obliged him.

I did not weep, and I did not shout. I remember being surprised at how orderly my hands were. I rose, and I took off my boots and set them side by side under the bed, as a man does who means to be back. Then I put my hand into the breast of my coat and drew out the bell-rope knife.

It had a short blade, bone-handled, worn thin as a leaf on the whetstone. I had cut a thousand ends of rope with it, and I had never once held it for any other purpose. I held it now. I turned it to the window and the grey began to lie along the edge, and I said aloud, quite quietly, "I have drowned nobody," and the tube in the wall took the words and carried them down.

I unlocked the door and opened it on its stiff hinge, a half-inch at a time. The stair ran down into the dark, and I went down it in my stockings, one hand on the wall, the knife held against my thigh. The sixth tread cried out and I stood on it, and stood, until the house settled. Below me, under the parlour door, lay a long thin line of lamplight.

He was awake. At four in the morning, in a house of sleepers, Reginald Wetherby was awake, and waiting, and I heard him turn a page.

• • •

I pushed the door, and it went inward without a sound, as if it had been oiled for the purpose.

The parlour was warm. A fire of sea-coal burned low in the grate, and the lamp stood on the table at his elbow, turned up high and trimmed clean. Reginald Wetherby sat in the horsehair chair with a ledger open across his knee and a cup of tea going cold on the arm. He did not rise. He did not so much as lift the hand that held the page. He looked at the knife, and then at my stockinged feet, and then he sighed, as a man sighs at a clock that has been wrongly wound.

"You will want to put that down, Mr. Marchbanks, before you cut yourself on your own conclusions. Sit, if you like. The chair by the dresser is sound."

I did not sit. I said, "You have been listening to me sleep."

"Eleven months," said Wetherby. "You talk a great deal, for a quiet man. Your father's debt, the bell, a boat, the black water off the Mire stairs. Mr. Fothergill has a gift for arrangement. He took what you gave us and made it speak in order."

"There was no drowning."

"There was a confession." He turned a leaf. "Your father's note is a curious instrument, Mr. Marchbanks. It may be called in from a ringer of St. Anselm's only if that ringer has stood convicted, or confessed, of a crime. I did not draw it. I merely hold it. A man must be patient, and then he must be helpful."

"I never signed anything."

"You signed on the fourteenth, in the vestry, a receipt for the new sally. You were very tired. The paper beneath it was a fair copy of what you had dictated to us, in your own voice, every night since Michaelmas. Mr. Fothergill read it into the horn and you answered, and I wrote it down." He closed the ledger on his finger. "It was sold to the magistrate yesterday afternoon. He is an early man. He will be here at dawn."

I think I raised the knife. I know that Wetherby watched it rise, and that he did not move. The fire ticked in the grate. I understood, with perfect orderly clearness, that he was not afraid, because there was nothing left in me that he needed to fear.

I ran. The sixth tread cried out and I did not stop for it. I reached the landing, and the garret door stood open as I had left it. I had one foot across the sill when I heard the stair behind me take a slow, deliberate weight, and the door came away from my hand and shut. The key turned. I heard it go round twice, and then withdrawn, and then the steady descent of a man who has no reason to hurry.

I sat on the bed. The window had gone the colour of old pewter, and the fog pressed its face to the glass. I laid the knife in my lap, blade toward my knees. On the sill the phonograph clicked. The stylus lifted from its rest, swung out, and dropped by itself into the wax, and my own voice, tender and ruined, began once more to say how sorry I was for the drowning.

item.title: Ten Minutes Fast
item.description: A grieving chimney sweep is hired to clear every flue at a manor waiting for auction, and in the nursery he finds a clock that runs ten minutes fast. Tiny handprints in old soot and a penny whistle hidden in the brick suggest the clock isn't wrong at all, and that whatever it's counting toward is nearly here.
item.content:encoded:
I came to Wetherby Grange on the last Tuesday in October, with my rods tied in a bundle across my shoulder and my brushes wrapped in sacking. I had buried my wife, Ellen, in the spring, and since then I had taken any work that paid in coin and asked no conversation of me. The lane was rutted and the gates stood open on one hinge. Every window on the east front had its shutter drawn, and the gravel before the porch was printed with cart wheels where the dealers had already been.

Mr Fennimore, the auctioneer, met me in the hall. He was a broad man in a grey waistcoat, and he held a pencil behind his ear and a printed catalogue against his chest. Each of the lots had a paper ticket tied to it with string: the hall stand, the barometer, the brass fender, the very coal scuttle by the door.

"Cardew, is it? Maurice Cardew?" He laughed. "We share a Christian name, then. Every flue in the house, mind. Twenty-two of them. The buyers will want to light fires and see them draw before they bid on a single grate."

I asked him where I should begin, and he took me up the back stair to the nursery, which was at the top of the house under the slates. The room smelled of damp plaster and mouse. There was a rocking horse with no tail, a narrow iron bed stripped to its webbing, and against the far wall a longcase clock in a brass-bound case, taller than I was. Its brass face was painted with a ship and a moon, and its pendulum swung behind a little pane of glass with a slow, dry knock.

"That one runs ten minutes fast," said Mr Fennimore, and laughed again. "Always has, they tell me. Nobody's ever mended it. It won't fetch a shilling."

He went down to his ledgers. I stood a long while before the clock. I had no money for fine things, but I had my fee coming, and I thought a clock that no one wanted might go for the price of a pint and a pie. I saw it in the corner of my room in Tanner's Row. I heard it knocking there of a night, where there was otherwise nothing to hear. Before I had even unpacked a brush, I had counted it mine.

I spread my sheets across the hearth and weighted them with bricks from the yard. I screwed the first rod into the head of the brush and pushed it up into the dark, then the second rod, then the third, twisting as I went. Soot came down in a long sigh and settled on the sheet. It was old soot, dry as snuff, and it smelled of nothing at all.

When I drew the brush back out and knelt to fold the cloth, I stopped.

The soot had come down in flat cakes, the way it does when it has lain undisturbed for many years. Pressed into every cake was the shape of a small hand, fingers spread, thumb splayed outward. There were dozens of them, and each one was turned so that the fingers pointed up the flue.

Behind me, the clock struck the quarter, ten minutes before its time.

• • •

I did not call out. I folded the sheet with the hands inside it, corner over corner, and laid it by the fender, and I told myself that soot will take any shape a tired man cares to give it. Then I went into the hearth myself.

The nursery flue was wide at the throat, wider than any I had swept in Lambeth or Southwark, wide enough for a grown man to stand in with his head bent. I lit my stub of candle and stood up into it. The brick was cold and furred. Above the smoke-shelf it narrowed, and there, at the height of my raised hand, I found a ledge where a brick had been left out of the course. Something lay in the gap. I closed my fingers on it and brought it down into the light.

It was a tin whistle, a penny toy, dented along one side as though it had been bitten. The mouthpiece was black. When I turned it over, a little soot ran out of the finger-holes and onto my wrist.

"You found his whistle, then."

The porter stood in the doorway with a lot ticket in one hand and a pot of paste in the other. He was a lad of eighteen or nineteen, Harold Pennington by name, all elbows, with a clean collar he was plainly proud of. He came in and looked at the toy in my palm without touching it.

"Whose whistle?" I said.

"The boy's. Old Mr Lark's climbing boy, the first master here. Everyone in the village knows it." He set down his paste. "Mrs Lark was lying sick in this very room, in eighteen fifty-one, and Lark sent the boy up to clear the stack so she'd have a fire. And the boy got up top and sat there whistling, the way they did, to say he'd come out. Only she died while he was whistling. Lark said he'd whistled her soul up the chimney. So he had the hearth bricked over that same night, with the boy still inside."

While he talked, I looked past him at the clock. I had looked at it when I came in from the yard, and I had marked then that it showed four minutes to four, and I had marked too that it was right, for I had set my own watch by the church at Hollins Cross that morning. I had thought nothing of it. A clock that strikes early may still be right by chance.

"They opened it again when Lark was buried," said Pennington. "Found nothing. Not so much as a button."

The minute hand moved. It did not tick. It slid, smoothly, as if a finger behind the dial were pushing it, past the hour and on, and it stopped at ten past four.

I took out my watch. The case was warm from my waistcoat. Four o'clock exactly. I held it to my ear and heard it going.

"It's fast," said Pennington, following my eyes. "Mr Fennimore told you."

"It isn't fast," I said. "It was right a moment since."

He laughed, not unkindly, and picked up his paste again. But I knew it then, as surely as I knew the weight of the whistle in my hand. That clock had never once been wrong. For seventy years it had been telling the hour of something that had not happened yet, and it had stood here in the dark nursery, waiting for the rest of us to catch it up.

Ten minutes. I closed my hand round the whistle and found that the black on the mouthpiece was wet.

• • •

I wiped my thumb across it and the thumb came away black. I did not look to see whether the black was soot or something thinner. I put the whistle in my waistcoat pocket, against the watch, and I went down the back stairs with my brushes still in the nursery grate.

Fennimore was in the long gallery with his ledger open on a sideboard, chalking lot numbers onto the feet of chairs. He had his spectacles pushed up onto his forehead and a stub of chalk behind one ear.

"Done already, Cardew?"

"I'm done," I said. "I'll take what's owed for the kitchens and the east wing, and you can find another man for the nursery."

He chalked a seven onto a walnut leg before he answered. "You'll take nothing. The terms were every flue in the house. The buyers want the stacks sound before they'll bid on the fabric." He blew the chalk dust off his fingers. "Every flue, Mr Cardew. Not every flue but one."

"There's a fault in it. The brick is rotten."

"Then clear it and say so in your note, and I'll put it in the catalogue." He looked at me over the ledger. "And the clock goes under the hammer at five, if you still fancy it. I'll not hold it back for a man who walked off the job."

I stood there with my hands hanging. I could smell my own clothes, the sour char of forty years of other men's fires. I thought of the clock's brass face in the nursery, and of the shilling I had already counted out in my head, and of the rent on my room in Tanner's Row. I said nothing. I turned and went back up the stairs, and I knew, even as I climbed them, that I had been meant to turn.

Pennington had gone to the window with his paste pot and was smoothing a lot ticket onto the rocking horse. He did not look round. The clock stood where it had stood. Ten past four. My watch said six minutes past.

I knelt on the hearthstone and put my head and shoulders into the flue. The cold came down onto my neck. I took the whistle out of my pocket and held it in front of my face, though I could not see it, and I told myself plainly that it was a penny toy, tin and solder, and that a man of fifty-three does not go in fear of a toy. I put it to my lips and blew.

It made a thin, cracked note, very short. The note went up the stack and did not come back down. I listened for the echo off the brick and there was none. Somewhere above me, a long way above, a little grit pattered loose and fell on my cheek.

"Mr Cardew?" said Pennington behind me. "Was that you?"

I fumbled for my watch and tilted its face to the grey light coming past my shoulder. Nine minutes past four.

The brick above me groaned like a door on a dry hinge. Then the whole throat of the chimney came down onto my back, brick and mortar and a hundredweight of soot, and drove me flat into the grate. I could not breathe. I could not see. The weight lay on me from my shoulders to my hips, and in the black, close against my ear, something small began to scratch at the brick, working its way down.

• • •

The scratching came nearer. It was a patient sound, like a fingernail worked into mortar, and it stopped an inch from my ear. Then something took hold of my ankles.

It was Pennington. I knew his grip, a grown man's hand, broad and warm through my stockings. I knew his voice too, which kept saying, "Hold on, Mr Cardew, hold on," as if I could do anything else. He set his boots against the fender and pulled. The bricks dragged at my coat. My chin scraped across the iron bars of the grate and I felt the skin tear. He pulled again, grunting, and I came out of the chimney all at once in a slide of soot and broken mortar. I lay on the hearthstones with my mouth full of grit.

I coughed until I could see. The first thing I saw was the clock.

It stood against the far wall in the grey light from the window. Its brass face was dull with dust, and its hands had not moved. Ten past four. When I dragged my watch out, it said nine minutes past and some seconds more. I was out. I was breathing. The flue had come down and spat me out alive, and the clock had not so much as twitched.

I understood it then, lying there. I will set it down plainly, because I have had a long while since to think about it. The house had never wanted me. The fall was not meant to kill me. It was meant to bring someone else to the hearth.

Pennington was kneeling over me with his face streaked black and his hand held out. "Can you stand, sir? Take my wrist. Come on, now." I took it. His wrist was thin, and the pulse jumped in it under my thumb. He was nineteen, perhaps twenty. That afternoon he had told me his mother kept a cookshop in Leeds.

Behind his shoulder the mouth of the chimney stood open and black, wider than before. Out of the black came two hands.

They were small, no bigger than my palm. They were black to the wrist with old soot, with long fingers and broken nails, and they came down slowly, feeling along the brick. I watched them as closely as I had watched the minute hand that afternoon. They found the back of Pennington's collar and closed on it.

At first he did not feel them. He was still pulling me up and saying, "That's it, that's it," and I was half on my feet with my weight on his arm.

I let go of his wrist.

I do not say I pushed him. I opened my hand, that is all. Then I stepped back across the boards to the clock and laid my palm flat against the warm brass of its case. I could feel the pendulum through it, steady and unhurried. Pennington stared at me with his mouth open. Then the hands pulled, and he went over backwards into the grate.

His heels drummed on the hearthstone. His fingers caught the edge of the mantel and slipped off. He did not scream, because there was no room for it. The chimney took him in by the shoulders, then the chest, then the hips. I heard his knees knock on the brick as he went up. Above the knocking, very faint and very high, someone began to whistle.

• • •

The whistling went on for perhaps three notes, thin and pleased, and then it stopped. Something shifted in the flue, a slow scrape of cloth on brick, and a little dry soot came pattering down onto the hearthstones. Then the first boot fell. It was a hobnailed boot with the lace still tied, and it struck the iron of the grate and lay on its side. I counted. I do not know why I counted, but I reached seven before the second one came down and landed on top of the first, toe to heel, as neatly as if a man had set them out to be blacked.

Under my palm the clock gave a small click, like a latch dropping into its keep. I looked up. The minute hand had gone back. It stood a hair past the twelve, at one minute after four, and my own watch, when I drew it out on its chain, said the same. The pendulum swung on as before. Nothing in the room had moved except the boots and the hands of the clock.

I went to the washstand and poured what water was left in the jug over my hands. It came off grey, then black, and I wiped my fingers on my trousers and found they were black still.

Fennimore came up the nursery stairs at a quarter past by the clock. He had his catalogue under his arm and a pencil behind his ear, and he stopped in the doorway with his nose wrinkled at the soot.

"Where's Pennington got to? I've two men waiting on the dining chairs."

"He never came up," I said.

"He told Mrs Garside he was coming up to you."

"Then he told her wrong. I've been alone with this flue the whole hour, and it's come down on me, as you can see." I pointed at the heap of brick in the grate. The boots lay under it, and only one heel showed, and it might have been any old thing left behind by a careless house.

Fennimore sucked his teeth and wrote something in his catalogue. "The flue's your affair. I'll not pay for half a job."

"Then pay me nothing," I said. "Give me the clock instead. I'll bid you a shilling for it now, and save you the trouble of five o'clock."

He laughed at that, the same laugh as in the morning, and looked at the clock as though it had insulted him. "A shilling. You're welcome to it, Cardew, and the dust inside it."

I paid him out of my waistcoat pocket and he went down the stairs calling for Pennington.

The carter brought it to my lodgings in Tanner's Row after dark, wrapped in a horse blanket, and it took the two of us to stand it against the wall by my bed. When he had gone I lit the candle and opened the case. The key hung inside on a hook. I fitted it to the winding square and turned it, eight turns, and each turn left a black thumbprint on the brass face. I had washed my hands three times on the road home. I shut the little glass door and sat on the bed with my boots off.

The clock said nine minutes past ten. My watch said the same. I watched the minute hand, and it moved to ten past, and then it moved again, though the pendulum had not swung, and the room was silent, and it crept on over the black marks of my fingers until it stopped, and stood, at a quarter past.
